lessons.title: 1. MVI fundamentals
lessons.summary: The three pillars of the pattern and how it differs from MVVM

blocks.text: MVI (Model – View – Intent) is a way to organize a screen where state is single, immutable, and every change to it has a name.
The three pillars

rows: The whole screen is described by one State object

blocks.code:
dispatch(Intent)          reduce(State, Intent)
View ──────────────► Store ──────────────────────────► State ──► View
                       │
                       └── I/O ──► Intent.Internal(result) ──► reduce
blocks.caption: Data flow

blocks.text: How is this different from MVVM?

In MVVM you usually have several StateFlows and many public methods (**load()**, **onSearch()**, **toggleFavorite()**), each mutating state in its own way. In MVI there is one entry point (**dispatch**) and one place where mutation happens (the reducer).
If you see `_state.value = ...` in five places in a ViewModel, that is not MVI — it is MVVM with a data class.
Splitting intents — the crucial part

blocks.caption: UsersContract.kt

blocks.text: The result of a network request does **not** set state directly — it returns to the loop as Intent.Internal and goes through the same reducer. That way every state change is named and visible on the timeline.
Open the Demo tab, expand “Intent timeline”, and type something into the search field. Count how many intents are created by a single search.

lessons.title: 2. MVI in practice
lessons.summary: Effects, optimistic updates, debounce, time travel

blocks.text: a) One-off effects

Snackbars and navigation **must not** be fields in state. State is replayable — after a screen rotation the snackbar would be shown a second time. Effects travel through a separate channel and are consumed exactly once.
b) Optimistic update with rollback
Tapping the star changes the UI immediately, before the server responds. If the server rejects the operation, we roll the change back.

blocks.code:
is UsersIntent.Ui.FavoriteToggled ->
    if (intent.userId in state.savingFavorites) state   // protection against double-clicking
    else state.copy(users = state.users.toggleFavorite(intent.userId))

is UsersIntent.Internal.FavoriteSaveFailed ->           // server rejected it
    state.copy(users = state.users.toggleFavorite(intent.userId))
blocks.caption: UsersReducer.kt

blocks.text: In the Demo tab, user **Damian Zieliński** always rejects saving — tap his star to see the rollback and the message.
c) Debounce and canceling stale requests

blocks.caption: UsersViewModel.kt

blocks.text: collectLatest protects against a classic search bug: an older query result overwriting a newer one.
d) Derived state computed in State

blocks.code:
val showEmptyState: Boolean
    get() = !isLoading && error == null && users.isEmpty()

blocks.text: The “empty screen” condition is defined once and testable without UI. You cannot forget it in one of three places that render the list.
e) Time travel

Since every change is reduce(state, intent), the history of (intent, state) pairs describes the whole session. In the Demo tab, click an entry on the timeline — the UI will return exactly to that state.
In Demo, turn on “Simulate network error”, refresh the list, and then go back on the timeline to the state before the error.

lessons.title: 3. MVP vs MVVM vs MVI
lessons.summary: The evolution of presentation patterns and what each step actually changes

blocks.text: All these patterns answer the same question: **where to keep screen logic so it does not end up in the Activity**. They differ in how the View learns about changes.

rows: Presenter calls View methods through an interface
Hundreds of methods in the View interface

blocks.text: MVC — the starting point
On Android, the Activity used to be both the controller and the view. The result: 2,000-line files, business logic tangled with the lifecycle, and tests only on a device.
MVP — the Presenter tells the View what to do

blocks.caption: The same screen in MVP

blocks.text: **Advantage:** logic moved out of the Activity and can be tested (you provide a fake View). **Drawback:** the presenter must remember to call *every* combination of methods. Forget `hideLoading()` in one branch and the spinner stays on screen forever.
MVP problem: screen state exists only as a history of method calls. It cannot be read or serialized.
MVVM — the View observes data

blocks.caption: The same screen in MVVM

blocks.text: **Advantage:** no reference to the View, survives screen rotation, integrates beautifully with Compose. **Drawback:** three independent streams may enter a combination you never designed — for example `isLoading = true` **and** a visible error **and** the old list at the same time.
MVVM problem: scattered mutation. Each public method changes state in its own way, so there is no single place where all transitions are visible.
MVI — one state, one entry point, one place of mutation

blocks.caption: The same screen in MVI (our project)

blocks.text: Impossible combinations disappear because `LoadSucceeded` **always** turns the loader off and clears the error. You cannot forget it, because it is one line in one place.
Comparison across three dimensions
When NOT to use MVI

items: A static screen (terms, “about app”) — MVI is unnecessary overhead.
A form with 30 fields — consider one Intent with the whole form model instead of 30 separate intents.
A team that is not in the habit of writing tests — the biggest benefit of MVI (testability) will go unused.

blocks.text: MVI is not “better MVVM”; it is MVVM with imposed discipline: one state, one entry point, one transition function.
Take `UsersViewModel` from this project and write down how many places mutate state. Then do the same for any MVVM ViewModel from your work.

lessons.title: 4. Clean Architecture — theory
lessons.summary: The dependency rule, layers, ports and adapters

blocks.text: Clean Architecture (Robert C. Martin) is a way to divide code into concentrically arranged layers. The whole pattern boils down to one rule.
The dependency rule: source code may depend only inward. An inner layer knows nothing about an outer layer.
Layers from the inside out

rows: Calling the API while bypassing the domain

blocks.text: Ports and adapters
The domain defines a **port** — an interface describing what it needs. The data layer provides an **adapter** — a concrete implementation. This is the Dependency Inversion Principle (the D in SOLID).

blocks.caption: Port — domain/repository/UserRepository.kt
Adapter — data/repository/InMemoryUserRepository.kt

blocks.text: The dependency arrow points **inward**: `data` knows about `domain`, never the other way around. That is why replacing the data source does not touch business rules.
Why all this? Three concrete gains

items: Replaceability: swapping a fake for Ktor is a one-line change in the DI module.
Testability: you test business rules without network, database, or UI.
Sharing: the same domain runs on Android and iOS unchanged.

blocks.text: Clean Architecture is not about the number of folders, but the direction of dependency arrows. You can have 20 packages and zero clean architecture.

lessons.title: 5. Clean Architecture in this project
lessons.summary: Concrete files, request flow, and common mistakes

blocks.code:
core/mvi/          MVI framework (feature-independent)
domain/
  model/           User – pure Kotlin
  repository/      PORTS: UserRepository, NetworkFailureSwitch
  usecase/         SearchUsersUseCase, SetFavoriteUseCase
data/repository/   ADAPTER: InMemoryUserRepository
presentation/
  users/           Contract, Reducer, ViewModel, Screen
  learn/           this learning screen
di/                Koin modules
blocks.caption: Structure of shared/src/commonMain

blocks.text: Why a use case if it is one line?

blocks.caption: domain/usecase/SearchUsersUseCase.kt

blocks.text: The rule “favorites at the top, then alphabetically” is **business** logic, not presentation logic. If it lived in the ViewModel, it could not be reused in a widget or on iOS without copying.
Flow of one request through the layers

items: 1. UI: dispatch(Ui.QueryChanged("An")) — presentation
2. Reducer: state.copy(query = "An") — presentation, pure function
3. ViewModel: debounce → call the use case — presentation
4. SearchUsersUseCase: sorting rule — domain
5. UserRepository (port) → InMemoryUserRepository (adapter) — data
6. Result returns as Internal.LoadSucceeded → reducer → new state

blocks.text: Common mistakes we avoid here

rows: Business rules cannot be tested or shared
Changing a field in the API forces changes across the whole app
Repository interface in the data layer
Reverses the dependency direction — the domain starts depending on data
Untestable without UI and easy to duplicate

blocks.text: Check in the code: does any file in domain/ import anything from data/ or presentation/? (Answer: no — and that is the whole point.)
Write a UserRepository implementation backed by Ktor and swap it in DataModule. Count how many files outside data/ and di/ you had to change.

lessons.title: 6. Kotlin type declarations: enum vs sealed
lessons.summary: Which construct models which idea, and why the wrong choice hurts later

blocks.text: Kotlin offers an unusually rich set of type declarations, and most of the confusion comes from two that look interchangeable: `enum class` and `sealed`. They are not. One models a **fixed set of values**, the other a **fixed set of shapes**.
Ask what varies. If only the name varies, use an enum. If the data varies from case to case, use sealed.
The whole family, briefly

rows: A value — equals, hashCode, copy for free
A typed wrapper with no allocation
A closed set of named constants

blocks.text: `sealed interface` is usually preferable to `sealed class`: a class can implement several interfaces but inherit from only one class, so interfaces allow crossing hierarchies. This project uses `sealed interface` almost everywhere and `sealed class` only for `UserSyncException`, which must extend `Exception`.
The core difference

blocks.caption: Both are from this project

blocks.text: `QuizCategory` needs nothing but a name, so an enum is exactly right. A `Block` carries different data in every case — a paragraph has text, a table has rows — and an enum simply cannot express that.
Side by side
Exhaustiveness: the property both share
Both make `when` exhaustive without an `else` branch, and that is the point. Adding a case breaks compilation at every place that has to handle it — the compiler produces the to-do list.

blocks.caption: QuizLabels.kt

blocks.text: Never add `else` to a `when` over an enum or a sealed type just to silence the compiler. That single line converts every future compile error into a silent runtime bug.
When an enum is the right call
An enum is not merely a list of names — entries can carry properties and implement interfaces, as long as **every** entry has the same shape.

blocks.caption: Route.kt

blocks.text: `entries` is what settles it. A sealed hierarchy has no built-in way to enumerate its subtypes, so a bottom bar built on sealed would need a hand-maintained list — and a list that someone will forget to update.
When sealed is the right call

blocks.caption: UiText.kt

blocks.text: The two cases carry completely different data. As an enum this would collapse into one class with a nullable field for every variant — the classic “bag of optionals”, where invalid combinations become representable and every reader has to guess which fields are set.
Sealed types make illegal states unrepresentable. An enum with five nullable fields makes them merely unlikely.
Nesting: the trick behind MVI intents

blocks.caption: UsersContract.kt

blocks.text: A nested sealed hierarchy lets a single `when` in the reducer stay exhaustive while the store filters on the intermediate type. An enum offers nothing comparable: it is flat by construction.
data object, and why it matters
For a stateless case inside a sealed hierarchy, prefer `data object`: it generates a sensible `toString()` and `equals()`. Debug output, logs and the intent timeline all depend on it.
Traps worth knowing

items: **Enum entries are eagerly initialised singletons.** The whole enum loads on first touch of any entry, so a heavy initialiser is paid for even by code touching one constant.
**ordinal is not a stable identifier.** Reordering entries silently changes it, so never persist or transmit `ordinal` — persist `name`.
**Enums cannot be generic**; sealed types can. A `Result<T>` has to be sealed.
**Sealed subtypes must live in the same module** (same package before Kotlin 1.5). That is what makes exhaustiveness sound.
**Serialization differs.** An enum serialises by name; a sealed hierarchy needs a discriminator, which is why the DTOs here declare `@SerialName("paragraph")` and a `classDiscriminator`.

blocks.text: Serialization in practice

blocks.caption: LessonDto.kt

blocks.text: The enum equivalent needs no ceremony — `"category": "mvi"` is the whole story. That asymmetry is a real argument for an enum whenever the wire format is simple.
Deciding in ten seconds

items: Does every case carry the same data (or none)? → **enum**
Does the code need to iterate all cases? → **enum**
Do the cases carry different data? → **sealed**
Do you need generics or nesting? → **sealed**
Does one case need multiple distinct instances? → **sealed**

blocks.text: And when both would work — a flat set of cases with identical data — pick the enum. It is shorter, it iterates for free, it survives interop with Swift, and it serialises without configuration.
Find QuizCategory and Block in this project. For each, argue why converting it to the other construct would make the code worse.

Take UsersState and try to express it as an enum of screen states (Loading, Content, Error). Notice what happens to the data each state needs — and why the project keeps a data class with derived properties instead.

lessons.title: 7. Abstract class vs interface
lessons.summary: What each one can declare, and why the wrong choice is hard to undo

blocks.text: Both an `abstract class` and an `interface` describe something incomplete: they declare members without implementing all of them, and neither can be instantiated. The similarity ends there. An interface says **what a type can do**; an abstract class says **what a family of types already is**.
Interface for a capability that unrelated types can have. Abstract class for a partially built thing whose subclasses are variations of one idea.
Side by side

rows: abstract, or with a custom getter

blocks.text: The first row is the one that decides most designs. Single inheritance is a budget: a type can spend it only once, so an abstract class should be reserved for the one thing that genuinely defines what the type *is*.
An interface can have bodies — it just cannot have state

Kotlin interfaces may implement methods and declare properties, which surprises people who arrive from older Java. What they cannot do is hold a value: an interface property has no backing field, so it must be recomputed by a getter on every access.

blocks.caption: The dividing line: behaviour is shareable, state is not

blocks.text: Constructors: the difference that is easy to miss

An abstract class has a constructor, so it can demand its dependencies up front and guarantee an invariant before any subclass code runs. An interface has no such moment — every implementor is responsible for its own setup, and there is no way to force it.

blocks.caption: MviStore.kt

blocks.text: Try to express that as an interface and three things break at once: the mutable state flow has nowhere to live, `protected` is unavailable, and the class can no longer extend `ViewModel` through the same declaration.
The mirror image: ports are interfaces

blocks.caption: KeyValueStore.kt

blocks.text: An abstract `KeyValueStore` would be a mistake even though it would compile. SharedPreferences and NSUserDefaults share no implementation worth inheriting, and forcing a common base would spend the single inheritance slot of every adapter on a class that contributes nothing.
Depend on interfaces, inherit from abstract classes only for shared implementation. A dependency expressed as an abstract class is a dependency on someone else's code, not on a contract.
Why this matters for tests

A fake that implements an interface is a few lines and has no behaviour it did not opt into. A fake that extends an abstract class inherits everything the base does — its constructor requirements, its state, its side effects — and the test ends up exercising the base as much as the subject.
Diamonds, and what Kotlin does about them

Multiple interfaces may supply the same default body. Kotlin refuses to guess: the implementor must override the member and choose explicitly with `super<Type>`, so the ambiguity is resolved in source rather than at runtime. Abstract classes avoid the question entirely — there is only ever one of them.
In a multiplatform project

A Kotlin interface becomes a Swift protocol and an abstract class becomes a Swift class, which inherits Swift's own single-inheritance rule. A deep abstract hierarchy in shared code is therefore a constraint exported to iOS as well — one more reason to keep the shared surface made of interfaces.
And the third option: neither

Shared behaviour does not always need a supertype. An extension function, a small collaborator passed into the constructor, or a `sealed interface` with data-carrying subtypes often expresses the same thing without an inheritance relationship. Prefer composition; reach for an abstract class when several types genuinely share both state and behaviour.
Deciding in ten seconds

items: Do implementors need to be free to extend something else? → **interface**
Is this a boundary the app depends on (a port)? → **interface**
Do you need to store state or run a constructor? → **abstract class**
Do you need `protected` members? → **abstract class**
Would several types share real implementation *and* state? → **abstract class**
Is it shared behaviour with no state? → consider **neither** — an extension or a collaborator

blocks.text: When both would work, take the interface. It leaves the single inheritance slot unspent, it fakes cleanly in tests, and turning it into an abstract class later is a smaller change than untangling a hierarchy that should never have existed.
Find MviStore and KeyValueStore in this project. For each, list what would break if it were declared the other way — name the concrete member or dependency, not just the general principle.

Take UsersStore and try to move its shared loading logic into an abstract base class. Then try the same with a collaborator injected through the constructor. Compare how much of the base each test has to set up.

lessons.title: 8. Coroutines and Flow
lessons.summary: Scope, dispatcher, cancellation, StateFlow vs SharedFlow, cold and hot streams

blocks.text: A coroutine is a **resumable computation**: it can suspend at a `suspend` point and resume later without blocking a thread. That is why a thousand waiting coroutines cost a fraction of a thousand threads.
Concurrency ≠ parallelism. Coroutines give you concurrency even on a single thread — and that is exactly why races happen without multithreading.
suspend — what it really means

blocks.caption: Continuation Passing Style under the hood

blocks.text: A `suspend` function can be called only from another `suspend` function or from a coroutine. That is not a limitation — it is a guarantee that you will not accidentally suspend code that is not suitable for it.
Structured concurrency — the most important idea
Every coroutine has a **parent**. Canceling the parent cancels its children, and a child failure propagates upward. There are no orphans running in the background after the screen closes.

blocks.caption: viewModelScope in this project

rows: Grouping tasks inside a suspend function

blocks.text: GlobalScope is the equivalent of `new Thread()` without a reference. If you see it in a review, it is almost always a bug.
launch vs async
Rule: **`launch` when you do not need a result, `async` when you do**. If you do `async { }.await()` immediately on the next line, you are not parallelizing anything — use a regular call.
Dispatchers — where code actually runs
In well-written code, **a suspend function takes care of its own dispatcher** (`withContext(Dispatchers.IO)` inside the repository). The ViewModel should not know that something is a disk operation.
Rule: a suspend function should be safe to call from Dispatchers.Main. If it is not, that is a bug in the function, not in its caller.
Cancellation is cooperative

blocks.caption: This pattern is used in UsersViewModel

blocks.text: CancellationException is not a domain error; it is a control signal. Swallowing it breaks structured concurrency — the parent will think the child completed normally.
Flow — a stream of values
`Flow` is a **cold** stream: nothing happens until someone calls `collect`. Every collector starts its own execution.

blocks.code:
val numbers = flow {
    println("start")     // runs ONLY on collect
    emit(1)
    emit(2)
}

numbers.collect { }      // prints "start"
numbers.collect { }      // prints "start" a SECOND time

blocks.text: Cold vs hot — decision table

rows: Screen state — always has a value

blocks.caption: MviStore.kt — exactly this split

blocks.text: Do not keep one-off effects in StateFlow. State is replayable, so after a screen rotation the snackbar would be shown a second time.
Operators you must know

items: **map / filter** — transformation, as in collections.
**debounce(ms)** — waits for quiet; without it, a search box makes a request for every letter.
**distinctUntilChanged()** — skips consecutive duplicates.
**flatMapLatest** — cancels the previous stream when a new value arrives.
**collectLatest** — cancels previous processing when a new value arrives.
**combine** — combines several streams into one.
**catch** — handles stream errors without try/catch around collect.

blocks.code:
queryFlow
    .drop(1)                       // skip the initial value
    .debounce(350)                 // wait until the user stops typing
    .distinctUntilChanged()        // same query? do not repeat
    .collect { loadRequests.trySend(it) }

loadRequests.receiveAsFlow()
    .collectLatest { performLoad(it) }   // a new request cancels the old one
blocks.caption: UsersViewModel — full search chain

blocks.text: The three most common mistakes

rows: collect in onCreate without a scope

blocks.text: You can see the first one live in the **Sync** tab — the “StateFlow: .value = instead of update {}” scenario.
Open the Sync tab and run the “Lost update” scenario. Then open CoroutineConcurrencyLab.kt and see that the race is caused by a single `yield()`.
Add an `onEach { }` operator to UsersViewModel that logs every query and check in the console how many queries are created when typing quickly.

lessons.title: 9. RxJava vs Kotlin Flow
lessons.summary: Vocabulary, migration, and why Flow won on Android

blocks.text: RxJava was the standard for asynchrony on Android for years. It is worth knowing for two reasons: **you maintain legacy code** or **you read older libraries**. The concepts map almost one-to-one to Flow.
Vocabulary: Rx type → Kotlin equivalent

rows: Exactly one value or an error

blocks.text: The same code in both worlds

blocks.caption: RxJava
Kotlin Flow — equivalent

blocks.text: Operators: names differ, the idea does not
Why Flow won on Android

items: **Structured concurrency** — cancellation is inherited from the scope. In Rx you must remember `Disposable` manually; a forgotten `dispose()` is a classic leak.
**No `subscribeOn`/`observeOn`** — context is part of the coroutine, so you cannot accidentally run UI work on an IO thread.
**Readability** — `try/catch`, loops, and `if` work normally, without converting everything to operators.
**Kotlin Multiplatform** — Flow works on iOS; RxJava does not (it is a JVM library).
**Lower overhead** — no huge type hierarchy and no separate API for every case.

blocks.text: Rx is not “worse” — it is richer in operators and older. On Android it lost mainly because of manual subscription management and lack of KMP support.
What Rx has more of

items: Backpressure as a first-class concept (`Flowable` with strategies).
A very rich set of time-based operators (`window`, `buffer`, `throttleFirst`).
A mature `TestScheduler` and marble tests.

blocks.text: In Flow, some of this has to be assembled manually from `buffer()`, `conflate()`, and `sample()` — but in a typical mobile app it is rarely needed.
Migration step by step

items: Add `kotlinx-coroutines-rx3` — it provides bridges in both directions.
`single.await()` turns `Single<T>` into a value inside a coroutine.
`observable.asFlow()` turns an Rx stream into Flow.
`flow.asObservable()` goes the other way when legacy code requires it.
Migrate **from the presentation layer downward** — ViewModel first, then repositories.
Do not migrate everything at once; bridges allow coexistence.

blocks.caption: kotlinx-coroutines-rx3

blocks.text: Take the chain from UsersViewModel (debounce + collectLatest) and write its RxJava equivalent on paper. Notice how many places require manual cleanup.

lessons.title: 10. SOLID in practice
lessons.summary: The five principles using examples from this project — and what breaks without them

blocks.text: SOLID is five principles for class design. They are not dogma — they are a **diagnostic tool**: when code is hard to change or test, it usually violates one of them.
S — Single Responsibility
A class should have **one reason to change**. Not “do one thing”, but answer to one stakeholder.

blocks.caption: data/lesson/ and data/repository/

blocks.text: Sanity check: can you describe the class in one sentence without the word “and”? If not, it has too many responsibilities.
O — Open/Closed (open for extension, closed for modification)
Add new functionality by **adding code**, not rewriting existing code.

blocks.caption: domain/model/Lesson.kt

blocks.text: Watch the nuance: `sealed` **intentionally** forces `when` to be updated. That is not a violation of the principle; it is a conscious choice — the compiler points out all places instead of allowing a silent runtime bug.
L — Liskov Substitution
A subtype must be usable everywhere the base type is used — **without surprises**.

blocks.caption: UsersViewModelTest.kt

blocks.text: If substituting an implementation requires changing client code or adding `if (repo is X)`, the principle is broken.
I — Interface Segregation
Several narrow interfaces are better than one broad interface. A client should not depend on methods it does not use.

blocks.caption: di/DataModule.kt

blocks.text: Thanks to this, the production network implementation does not need to know anything about the failure switch — it simply does not implement that interface.
D — Dependency Inversion
High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on **abstractions**.
Key point: the interface lives in `domain`, not in `data`. If it lived in `data`, the dependency arrow would flip and the domain would start depending on an implementation detail.
SOLID and testability — what each principle gives you

rows: The test needs half the world in setup
Every change touches the same files
if (repo is Fake) in production code
A test needs the network or database

blocks.text: When to break them consciously

items: A prototype or spike you will throw away anyway.
Premature abstraction — an interface with one implementation “just in case” is a cost with no benefit.
Overzealous SRP leads to classes with one method and a thousand files; readability matters more than purity.

blocks.text: SOLID serves code changeability. If applying a principle makes code harder to understand and does not make anything easier — do not apply it.
Find the InMemoryUserRepository class in the project and write down how many reasons to change it has. Propose a split if network fetching were added to it.
Add a new content block type (for example Quote) and count how many files you had to change. That is a practical measurement of Open/Closed.

lessons.title: 11. Dependency Injection (Koin)
lessons.summary: Three modules = three layers, ViewModel scope

blocks.text: DI is the place where layers meet — the so-called composition root. Each layer has its own module.

blocks.caption: di/DataModule.kt

blocks.text: One instance is registered under two narrow interfaces. The rest of the app never sees the concrete class — that is the Interface Segregation Principle in configuration.

blocks.caption: di/DomainModule.kt and PresentationModule.kt

blocks.text: viewModel { } matters for MVI: if the store were recreated on every recomposition, we would lose state and the timeline.
The dependency graph is code too, and it can break too — that is why **KoinModulesTest** checks whether it can be resolved. A missing definition fails the test, not the user.

lessons.title: 12. Kotlin Multiplatform
lessons.summary: Source sets, targets, the memory model and how much is worth sharing

blocks.text: KMP shares **logic**, not necessarily the UI. That distinction is the whole point: the risky, complex part of an app is the business logic, and that is what stops being written twice.
KMP is not “write once, run anywhere”. It is “share what is worth sharing, stay native where it matters”.
Source sets: who sees what

blocks.code:
shared/src/
├─ commonMain/    every target — stdlib and multiplatform libraries only
├─ androidMain/   sees commonMain + the Android SDK
└─ iosMain/       sees commonMain + Apple frameworks
blocks.caption: The hierarchy in this project

blocks.text: `commonMain` compiles for every target, so it may only use APIs available everywhere. That is why `java.io.File`, `Context` and `java.time.LocalDate` are unavailable there — they are JVM or Android types.

rows: a port with a per-platform implementation

blocks.text: How much to share
Sharing is not all-or-nothing. Each layer is a separate decision, and the return on sharing falls as you move outward.

rows: Complex, and bugs here hurt everywhere
Testable logic; MVI makes it platform-free
Compose Multiplatform works, native UI is still a valid choice

blocks.text: Many teams share everything except the UI and keep SwiftUI on iOS. That is a legitimate architecture, not a half-measure — and it is exactly why the domain must not depend on Compose.
The memory model: the barrier that is gone

Kotlin/Native used to require `freeze()` before sharing an object between threads, and mutating a frozen object threw `InvalidMutabilityException`. That single rule made coroutines painful and was the most common reason teams abandoned KMP.
Since Kotlin 1.7.20 the new memory model removed freezing entirely. State is shared between threads as on the JVM, and coroutines behave the same on both platforms.
The practical consequence: advice written before 2022 about `freeze()`, `AtomicReference` and `@ThreadLocal` is obsolete. If you find it in a tutorial, check the date.
What Swift sees
The iOS framework is generated through Objective-C, and that interop layer is lossy. Knowing what gets lost prevents an unpleasant surprise at integration time.

rows: no direct equivalent — needs a wrapper
a protocol; switch requires a default branch
not visible — every parameter is required

blocks.text: Tools such as SKIE or KMP-NativeCoroutines generate idiomatic Swift on top of this — native enums with exhaustive matching, `AsyncSequence` instead of `Flow`. Worth reaching for before hand-writing wrappers.
Keep the exported API narrow. Every public type lands in the Objective-C header, inflating the framework and the compile time; a facade keeps the surface small and the interop tidy.
What KMP does not solve

items: **Platform behaviour still differs.** Permissions, background execution and lifecycles are not unified by sharing code.
**A shared bug ships twice.** The same defect now reaches both apps at once, which raises the value of tests rather than lowering it.
**Build times grow.** Every target is compiled separately; Kotlin/Native is the slow one.
**Library choice narrows.** A JVM-only dependency cannot enter commonMain, and that constraint shapes the architecture.

blocks.text: How this project is arranged

blocks.code:
commonMain/   core/mvi, domain, data, presentation, di  — ~95% of the code
androidMain/  SharedPreferences, Locale, WindowInsetsController
iosMain/      NSUserDefaults, NSLocale, the entry point
blocks.caption: Only genuinely platform-specific code lives outside commonMain

blocks.text: Everything platform-specific here is small and hidden behind a port. The result: `./gradlew :shared:iosSimulatorArm64Test` runs the very same tests as the Android ones — the logic is verified twice without being written twice.
Run ./gradlew :shared:iosSimulatorArm64Test and compare the test count with the Android run. The overlap is the measure of what is genuinely shared.
List everything in androidMain and iosMain in this project. Each file answers the question: what genuinely cannot be shared?

lessons.title: 13. Platform code: port or expect/actual?
lessons.summary: Two ways to abstract over a platform, and how to pick the right one

blocks.text: Sooner or later shared code needs something only a platform can provide: preferences, a locale, a window handle. Kotlin Multiplatform offers **two** mechanisms for that, and picking the wrong one is easy because both compile.
The question to ask is not “how do I call platform code” but “is there anything here worth substituting?”
Mechanism 1: expect/actual
`expect` declares a contract in `commonMain`, and each target supplies an `actual`. The compiler wires them together, and a missing `actual` is a compile error.

blocks.caption: SystemBars.kt in this project

blocks.text: Mechanism 2: a port plus DI
An ordinary interface in `commonMain`, implemented per platform and injected. No language feature involved — just Dependency Inversion applied to the platform boundary.

blocks.caption: KeyValueStore in this project

blocks.text: The difference that actually matters

rows: no — it is a global function

blocks.text: The decisive row is the second one. An `actual` **cannot be substituted**: there is exactly one per target, chosen by the compiler. Any test touching that code path drags in the real platform implementation — and on the JVM there is no Android window, so the test needs an emulator or does not run at all.
Why this project uses both
`KeyValueStore` and `LanguageProvider` are ports because their behaviour is worth substituting. `ThemePreferencesTest` runs entirely on the JVM in milliseconds:

`SystemBarsAppearance` is `expect/actual` because there is nothing to substitute. It has no branches, no return value and no logic — it hands a boolean to the platform. A fake would assert that a call happened, which tests the mock rather than the app.
A decision rule

items: Does it hold **state** or make a **decision**? Port.
Would a test want to **control** it (return a value, simulate a failure)? Port.
Is it a **one-way side effect** with no logic — vibrate, set a window flag, open a URL? `expect/actual` is fine.
Not sure? Choose the port. The cost is an interface; the cost of the wrong choice is an untestable code path.

blocks.text: `expect/actual` is a tool for filling gaps in the platform API, not for structuring an application. Structure comes from interfaces.
The trap: expect/actual for things that have logic

The same reasoning applies to random number generators, unique id factories and anything reading the network state. All of them look like “platform details” and all of them are decisions a test needs to control.
A middle ground worth knowing
A platform dependency does not have to be resolved by DI **or** by the compiler — it can simply be a parameter. This project passes the platform module into the entry point:

blocks.caption: App.kt

blocks.text: The dependency stays visible in the signature, `Context` never leaks into shared code, and previews get an in-memory default without any magic.
Find SystemBars.kt and its two actual implementations in this project. Consider what a test of that function could possibly assert — the answer explains why it is not a port.
Add a port that returns whether the device is online, with a fake for tests. Then try the same thing with expect/actual and compare how testable the result is.

lessons.title: 15. Types of tests in a mobile project
lessons.summary: Unit, smoke, golden, Espresso/Compose UI, XCTest and XCUITest

blocks.text: Tests differ in **cost** and **scope**. The test pyramid says: the higher you go, the slower, more expensive, and less stable tests become — so you should have fewer of them.

blocks.code:
╱╲          UI / E2E     — dozens, minutes
      ╱  ╲                        Espresso, Compose UI, XCUITest
     ╱────╲       Golden        — tens, seconds
    ╱      ╲                      Paparazzi, Roborazzi, snapshot
   ╱────────╲     Integration   — hundreds, seconds
  ╱          ╲                    ViewModel + fake repo
 ╱────────────╲   Unit          — thousands, milliseconds
╱______________╲                  reducer, use case
blocks.caption: Test pyramid

rows: Whether the most important paths are alive
Whether the UI looks the same
The whole app as the user sees it

blocks.text: 1. Unit tests — the foundation
In MVI the reducer is a pure function, so the test needs no coroutines, UI, or mocks. Write the most tests at this level.

blocks.caption: UsersReducerTest.kt (included in the project)

blocks.text: 2. Integration tests — ViewModel with dependencies
They verify collaboration: debounce, cancellation, retry, rollback. Time is virtual, so a 700 ms delay does not cost 700 ms.

blocks.caption: UsersViewModelTest.kt (included in the project)

blocks.text: 3. Smoke tests — whether the app is alive at all

A narrow set of tests run after every build: whether the DI graph can be assembled, whether the start screen renders, whether the main path passes. It should answer the question “is it worth running the rest of the tests”.

blocks.caption: Smoke DI — KoinModulesTest.kt (included in the project)

blocks.text: A smoke test is not a kind of technology, but a **role** of a test: quickly detect that the build is fundamentally broken.
4. Golden tests (screenshot / snapshot)

They render a component to a bitmap and compare it with an approved baseline (“golden file”). They catch visual regressions that no text assertion will catch: wrong padding, clipped text, wrong color in dark mode.

items: **Paparazzi** (Cash App) — renders on the JVM, without an emulator, very fast.
**Roborazzi** — based on Robolectric, works with Compose.
**Compose Preview Screenshot Testing** — official AGP tool.
**iOS: swift-snapshot-testing** (Point-Free) — equivalent for SwiftUI/UIKit.

blocks.caption: Sketch of a golden test (Paparazzi)

blocks.text: Golden tests work best with MVI: you provide a ready `State` and render. You do not have to click through half the app to reach an error state.
Practical note: approve golden files consciously. Mindless “update all snapshots” turns them into tests that always pass.
5. UI tests on Android — Espresso and Compose
**Espresso** is the classic tool for XML views. For Compose you use `ComposeTestRule` — the API is different, but the role is the same: we click and assert on the real UI tree.

blocks.caption: Espresso (XML views)
Compose UI test (equivalent for this project)

blocks.text: The project is ready for instrumentation tests: `shared/build.gradle.kts` configures `withDeviceTestBuilder` with `AndroidJUnitRunner`. Test code goes into the `androidDeviceTest` source set.

items: For stability, use `testTag("users_list")` instead of searching by text — text changes with translations.
Compose has automatic synchronization (idling); with manual timers, use `mainClock.advanceTimeBy(...)`.
Run UI tests selectively on CI — they are the slowest and most brittle.

blocks.text: 6. Tests on iOS — XCTest and XCUITest
**XCTest** is for unit tests of Swift code. **XCUITest** is for UI tests that drive the app from the outside — the equivalent of Espresso.

blocks.caption: XCUITest — iosApp/iosAppUITests

blocks.text: We test shared logic (reducer, use case) **once**, in Kotlin: `./gradlew :shared:iosSimulatorArm64Test` runs the same tests on the iOS simulator. Xcode then keeps only tests for the Swift and UI layers.
In KMP, do not duplicate logic tests in Swift. Test shared code once, and in Xcode verify what is actually iOS-specific.
What to run and when

blocks.code:
./gradlew :shared:testAndroidHostTest      # unit + integration + smoke (JVM)
./gradlew :shared:iosSimulatorArm64Test    # the same tests on iOS
./gradlew :androidApp:assembleDebug        # app build
./gradlew connectedAndroidTest             # instrumentation tests (requires an emulator)
# iOS UI: Xcode → Product → Test (⌘U)

MVI

items: The reducer is pure: no I/O, no time, no randomness.
The reducer knows WHAT happened; the ViewModel knows WHAT TO DO next.
Navigation and messages are effects, not state.
The I/O result returns as Intent.Internal — never `_state.value = ...`.
Derived state is computed in State, not in Compose.
Let CancellationException propagate — it is not a domain error.

blocks.text: Clean Architecture

items: Dependencies point inward: presentation → domain ← data.
Repository interface in domain, implementation in data.
A business rule belongs in a use case, not in the ViewModel.
The domain model is pure Kotlin — no framework annotations.
Test the DI graph just like the rest of the code.
